activity.title: We loved our time at the University of Maryland . What a weekend! Thank you, Oliver D'Esposito ( Startup Shell ) and Sammy Popat , for spreading the word as over 170 builders came together to take on the future of Spatial Intelligence, and the results were incredible. Winners: 1st Place ($10,000) - Construction Site Safety Intelligence Dashboard Rajveer Singh , Ananth Sriram , and Neel Mokaria The hackathon winners built and published a mini research paper on an AI-powered Construction Site Safety Intelligence Dashboard that turns egocentric footage into clear, per-worker safety reports at the end of each shift. The system automatically detects PPE compliance, flags ergonomic and proximity risks, and maps issues to OSHA standards, delivering practical, actionable insights without requiring live human monitoring. 2nd Place ($5,000) - DeepAnchor Vishal Kotha , Eshan Singh , Ankit Nakhawa , Souptik Mandal , Utsav Kataria The DeepAnchor team also published a mini research paper introducing a powerful idea: if AI can see standardized construction objects (like bricks or electrical boxes), it can use them as “anchors” to convert pixels into real-world measurements. DeepAnchor turns a single photo into a measurable scene by detecting known objects, calibrating a pixel-to-meter scale, and feeding structured measurements into a vision-language model to transform raw videos and images into clear, field-ready insights. 3rd Place ($2,500) - VISTA - Video Intelligence with Spatio-Temporal Augmented Retrieval for Egocentric Understanding Sneha Vellelath , Nithin Skantha Murugan , Santhi Prasanna , Shifa Mehreen , Swapnita Sahu The VISTA team published a mini research paper tackling a simple but powerful idea: today’s AI can see what’s in front of it, but it can’t remember what just happened. VISTA changes that by adding a “memory layer” to video and turning raw hardhat footage into a structured, searchable timeline of the physical world. Instead of scrubbing through hours of video, you can simply ask questions like “When did the electrician start rough-in?” or “Where is the scissor lift right now?” and get precise, time-stamped answers. Honorable Mentions: Splatt - ($1,000) Aneesh Reddy , Mohammad Sadiq , Farhan Kittur , Ian Coutinho , Vishal Shah Splatt took on the challenge of Spatial Intelligence in the Physical World and pushed it into full 3D. They built a system that turns everyday first-person construction videos into a living, navigable 3D model of the jobsite, mapping objects globally, tracking site changes over time, and enabling natural-language queries across the space. Experience Engine - ($1,000) Anjali Sreenivasan , Stephen Shkeda , Alex Woodka Experience Engine turns egocentric video into a map of muscle memory for construction, capturing how experienced workers move and make decisions instinctively, and transforming that hidden expertise into teachable, easy-to-digest insights. ...more ...more

Construction doesn’t have a labor problem. It has a black box problem. The first project I ran on my own, my boss handed me a budget and said, “This budget is your box. Live inside it. Plan the work, work the plan.” Then he gave me a stack of spreadsheets and wished me luck. The budget was never the problem. The problem was that the spreadsheets assumed the job would go exactly as planned. They didn’t account for the excavation delays and compressed anchor bolt install, the design info that showed up late, or the underground fire water tank that became a five-month out-of-sequence delay. The production reports told me weekly where I was. They never told me why I got there. That’s the black box of construction: everything that happens between production reports. It’s the gap between what happened and why it happened. The decisions, constraints, delays, and coordination challenges that no spreadsheet captures. Without visibility into that work, uncertainty compounds week over week until we get to the end of the job asking, How did we get here? or How are we going to finish strong? It sits between the estimate and the final cost, yesterday’s production and today’s, hours worked and work actually installed. Inside it are the decisions, delays, rework, and coordination failures that decide whether a crew succeeds or struggles. Yet we still try to run operations with accounting tools: hours in, quantities out. Then we wonder why productivity is so hard to improve. Last week our team was at the CII Elevate Summit in Denver. What stuck with me was a question that kept coming up: do we actually understand how work happens on site, not just what it costs? Because once you understand the why, everything downstream gets better: estimating, scheduling, forecasting, and the daily calls superintendents have to make. And crews spend less time fighting problems they didn’t create. Construction has never lacked hardworking people. We’ve always had exceptional builders. What we’ve lacked is visibility into the black box between planning and production. It’s time we stopped asking our people to outperform with bad information and started giving them better information instead. (That water tank taught me a lot about not giving up, I’ve been using that skill a lot these days)

“None of us is as smart as all of us.” Those words hung in the conference room at Telligent Masonry’s headquarters, and they perfectly capture what it means to build in this industry. A third-generation family business operating at such a high level doesn’t happen by accident. It’s built on discipline, commitment, and an unwavering focus on excellence. What impressed me most was that, after decades of success, the team still shows up every day looking for ways to improve, invest in their people, develop the next generation of craftsmen, and continue raising the bar. There is no “I” in the way they operate, only “we.” Last week, the team at Telligent Masonry, LLC opened their doors to us. We spent time in the field, walked jobsites, joined internal operations meetings, listened, asked questions, and worked side by side with their team to better understand how they drive operational excellence every day. We’re grateful for the opportunity to learn from exceptional builders and continue building tools that help teams operate safer, smarter, and more effectively. After starting to work together in April, we’ll continue expanding across Telligent’s workforce on projects throughout the East Coast over the coming months. By staying close to their teams, understanding how they operate, and learning from the field, we can help build technology that creates meaningful improvements in how work gets planned, executed, and measured. The construction industry is at an inflection point. Every company committed to building better is asking the same fundamental question: How do we take advantage of this moment? How do we operate 10x better than we did last year? The companies that embrace this opportunity will help define the next generation of construction. We’re grateful to partner with teams like Telligent that are committed to continuous improvement, investing in their people, and raising the standard for the industry. We’re just getting started.

This year has been a lot of changes. I walked into UMD not knowing a thing about how college would turn out, afraid of leaving home and more concerned that I’d hate the dining food than anything. And then… it worked out. I pushed myself into every chance I could to build on teams, to challenge myself and try something that I hadn’t before. Here’s what I did: - Did months of research at Algoverse into LLM Bias Steering, running hundreds of experiments on models of all sizes with thousands of prompts to learn why LLMs make decisions the way they do - Developed Testudo AI and now OneClique with the ACM, building an agent system from the ground up and collecting data for our campus search platform - Worked on Leasetudo for UMD’s TerpLabs, building a subleasing platform (pre-release) - Joined UMD’s App Dev club to work for IonQ and build improved UNet models for 13% F1 increases as an ML Engineer - Worked for QuarterMill (startup) for a month to build their MVP as Ingest and Infra Lead, ingesting thousands of documents for a massive graph database. - Attended 6 hackathons all in the Spring Semester, won $3000+ in my first two and kept building from there - And I applied to over 200 jobs, interviewed for a couple, finally ending up at Ironsite And that was just setting the stage for this summer. This summer, I’ve begun an internship as a Software Engineer Intern at Ironsite AI, working at a fast growing startup with engineers from Google Deepmind, Etched, Apple, and more, to build a product that’s for the boots, not the suits. It’s a mission I’m passionate about, and I can’t wait to be a part of it. I’m also in San Francisco, so I’m taking every opportunity I can get to venture into the startup world I can get. I already attended two hackathons in the last few days at WeaveHacks and Cursor x A16Z Night. I’ll be attending YC Startup School, YC’s internship fair, paper review nights, and nearly every luma event under the sun. The summer has just begun, but I’m ready to take it far. Thank you to Jeffrey Ju , Christopher Yung , Ben Gold , Max Mona , and the rest of the team at Ironsite for welcoming me in this summer. Looking forward to building for the built world!

Had a great time at Insurtech Insights last week in NYC! After speaking with professionals across the industry, one theme kept coming up: end-to-end automation. While everyone was confident in the value of their solutions, two major bottlenecks kept showing up— claims data standardization and legacy systems. At chromie.dev (YC S26) , we're focused on the second challenge. Many critical insurance workflows still depend on legacy portals that don't offer APIs, creating friction for automation. We're building reliable infrastructure to automate work across these systems and help teams move faster. Check us out 👉 https://chromie.dev/ Insurance demo 👉 https://lnkd.in/eECa8MpQ
